sourceDesc.p: The text of this edition is the Perseus Project's double-keyboarded transcription (c. 2003) of The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, ed. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright (Garden City, New York: Nelson Doubleday, Inc.), 2 vols. (OCLC 08687211; Tufts University's Tisch Library holds two catalog records for this set, both giving the date only as "19--"). Antony and Cleopatra is in volume 2, consulted in the Internet Archive copy bwb_S0-ATQ-198 (pp. 816-849); its date of printing is not confirmed. That edition reprints the Globe text in a setting of its own, with American spellings, which the transcription keeps. In some readings the transcription departs from both the copy-text and the Globe; the cause has not been established.

The Globe line numbering is not taken from the copy-text. It is read from two page-image witnesses to the Globe itself, printed from the same plates two decades apart: The Works of William Shakespeare, Cambridge and London: Macmillan, 1866 (HathiTrust miun.aba6868.0001.001, University of Michigan copy, catalog record 000241315) and The Works of William Shakespeare, London: Macmillan, 1887 (Internet Archive worksofwilliamsh0000shak_y3h8, Trent University copy, OCLC 1158473505).

editorialDecl.p: Words and structure -- divisions, speakers, speeches, stage directions, and verse lines where the copy-text sets verse -- are the double-keyboarded text, unaltered. Where a witness page disagrees with it over a word, the transcription stands and the disagreement is recorded in the project's reports.

The Globe lineation was regenerated from the witnesses in 2026. Each printed row of the witness page was classified by its typography, Globe lines were assembled from those rows, and the resulting count was checked on every page against every line number printed in that page's margins; a page whose count disagreed with any printed number was not accepted. Seventeen junctions in this play, where two speeches may share a verse line but the page's typography does not show whether they do, were decided individually, from the page images and, where the page is silent, from the line division of the Folger edition, Antony and Cleopatra, ed. Barbara A. Mowat and Paul Werstine, Folger Digital Texts, version 0.5 (Washington, DC: Folger Shakespeare Library, 2015), as distributed in the Shakespeare Drama Corpus (ShakeDraCor, play shake000035; github.com/dracor-org/shakedracor, commit c34c2d4). The Folger was consulted only for its division of shared lines, never for words or numbers. Each decision is recorded in the project's data tables.

The Globe line numbers previously carried by the Perseus edition were transcribed from the copy-text and are not retained. They are consistent with the numbering below, but were placed by a different convention.
First Folio through-line numbers are not carried by this edition. They remain in the Perseus P4 edition.

encodingDesc.p: <milestone unit="line" ed="Globe"> marks the first word of a Globe line, and every Globe line carries one, numbered. A Globe line may occupy more than one printed row: a verse line too long for the column, or a line shared between two speakers. <lb/> marks each printed row that begins no Globe line. A Globe milestone therefore also marks the start of a printed row, and reconstructing the page's rows requires reading both elements.

The @part attribute, which marks the parts of a verse line shared between speakers, is retained from the Perseus P4 edition and was not regenerated. It does not always agree with the Globe's division of shared lines; where the two differ, the Globe milestones govern the numbering.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Alexandria. A room in Cleopatra's
palace.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.p:
Nay, but this dotage of our general's O'erflows the measure: those his goodly eyes, That o'er the files and musters of the war Have glow'd like plated Mars, now bend, now
turn, The office and devotion of their view Upon a tawny front: his captain's heart, Which in the scuffles of great fights hath burst The buckles on his breast, reneges all temper, And is become the bellows and the fan To cool a gipsy's lust.
Flourish. Enter ANTONY, CLEOPATRA, her
Ladies, the Train, with Eunuchs fanning her.
Look, where they come: Take but good note, and you shall see in him. The triple pillar of the world transform'd Into a strumpet's fool: behold and see.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: If it be love indeed, tell me how much.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
There's beggary in the love that can be
reckon'd.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Then must thou needs find out new
heaven, new earth.
Enter an Attendant.

sp.speaker: Att.
sp.p: News, my good lord, from Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Grates me: the sum.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Nay, hear them, Antony: Fulvia perchance is angry; or, who knows If the scarce-bearded Cæsar have not sent His powerful mandate to you, 'Do this, or this; Take in that kingdom, and enfranchise that; Perform 't, or else we damn thee.'

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How, my love !

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Perchance! nay, and most like: You must not stay here longer, your dismission Is come from Cæsar; therefore hear it, Antony. Where's Fulvia's process ? Cæsar's I would say ?
both ? Call in the messengers. As I am Egypt's queen, Thou blushest, Antony; and that blood of thine Is Cæsar's homager: else so thy cheek pays
shame When shrill-tongued Fulvia scolds. The
messengers

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide
arch Of the ranged empire fall! Here is my space. Kingdoms are clay: our dungy earth alike Feeds beast as man: the nobleness of life Is to do thus; when such a mutual pair Embracing. And such a twain can do't, in which I bind, On pain of punishment, the world to weet We stand up peerless.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Excellent falsehood! Why did he marry Fulvia, and not love her ? I'll seem the fool I am not; Antony Will be himself.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
But stirr'd by Cleopatra. Now, for the love of Love and her soft hours, Let's not confound the time with conference
harsh: There's not a minute of our lives should stretch Without some pleasure now. What sport tonight ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Hear the ambassadors.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Fie, wrangling queen! Whom every thing becomes, to chide, to laugh, To weep; whose every passion fully strives To make itself, in thee, fair and admired! No messenger, but thine; and all alone To-night we'll wander through the streets and
note The qualities of people. Come, my queen; Last night you did desire it: speak not to us.
Exeunt Ant. and Cleo. with their train.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.p: Is Cæsar with Antonius prized so slight ?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.p: Sir, sometimes, when he is not Antony, He comes too short of that great property Which still should go with Antony.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.p: I am full sorry That he approves the common liar, who Thus speaks of him at Rome: but I will hope Of better deeds to-morrow. Rest you happy! Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Enter CHARMIAN, IRAS, ALEXAS, and a
Soothsayer.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, most any thing Alexas, almost most absolute Alexas, where's the soothsayer that you praised so to the queen? O, that I knew this husband, which, you say, must charge his horns with garlands !

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Soothsayer!

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Your will?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Is this the man ? Is't you, sir, that
know things ?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: In nature's infinite book of secrecy A little I can read.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p:
Show him your hand.
Enter ENOBARBUS.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Bring in the banquet quickly; wine
enough Cleopatra's health to drink.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good sir, give me good fortune.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: I make not, but foresee.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Pray, then, foresee me one.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: You shall be yet far fairer than you are.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: He means in flesh.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: No, you shall paint when you are old.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Wrinkles forbid!

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Vex not his prescience; be attentive.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Hush !

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p:
You shall be more beloving than
beloved.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I had rather heat my liver with drinking.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Nay, hear him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good now, some excellent fortune! Let me be married to three kings in a forenoon, and widow them all: let me have a child at fifty, to whom Herod of Jewry may do homage: find me to marry me with Octavius Cæsar, and companion me with my mistress.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p:
You shall outlive the lady whom you
serve.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
O excellent! I love long life better
than figs.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p:
You have seen and proved a fairer
former fortune Than that which is to approach.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Then belike my children shall have no names: prithee, how many boys and wenches must I have ?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: If every of your wishes had a womb, And fertile every wish, a million.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Out, fool! I forgive thee for a witch.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: You think none but your sheets are privy to your wishes.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Nay, come, tell Iras hers.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: We'll know all our fortunes.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Mine, and most of our fortunes, to night, shall be—drunk to bed.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: There's a palm presages chastity, if nothing else.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: E'en as the o'erflowing Nilus pre sageth famine.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Go, you wild bedfellow, you cannot soothsay.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Nay, if an oily palm be not a fruitful prognostication, I cannot scratch mine ear. Prithee, tell her but a worky-day fortune.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Your fortunes are alike.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: But how, but how ? give me particulars.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: I have said.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Am I not an inch of fortune better than she ?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Well, if you were but an inch of fortune better than I, where would you choose it?

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Not in my husband's nose.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Our worser thoughts heavens mend! Alexas,—come, his fortune, his fortune! O, let him marry a woman that cannot go, sweet Isis, I beseech thee! and let her die too, and give him a worse! and let worst follow worse, till the worst of all follow him laughing to his grave, fifty-fold a cuckold! Good Isis, hear me this prayer, though thou deny me a matter of more weight; good Isis, I beseech thee!

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Amen. Dear goddess, hear that prayer of the people! for, as it is a heartbreaking to see a handsome man loose-wived, so it is a deadly sorrow to behold a foul knave uncuckolded: therefore, dear Isis, keep decorum, and fortune him accordingly !

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Lo, now, if it lay in their hands to make me a cuckold, they would make themselves whores, but they'ld do't!

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Hush! here comes Antony.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Not he; the queen.
Enter CLEOPATRA.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Saw you my lord ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: No, lady.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Was he not here ?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
He was disposed to mirth; but on the
sudden A Roman thought hath struck him. Enobarbus!

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Madam ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Seek him, and bring him hither. Where's
Alexas ?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p:
Here, at your service. My lord
approaches.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
We will not look upon him: go with us.
Exeunt.
Enter ANTONY with a Messenger and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Fulvia thy wife first came into the field.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Against my brother Lucius ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Ay: But soon that war had end, and the time's state Made friends of them, joining their force 'gainst
Cæsar; Whose better issue in the war, from Italy, Upon the first encounter, drave them.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well, what worst ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
The nature of bad news infects the
teller.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: When it concerns the fool or coward. On: Things that are past are done with me. 'Tis thus: Who tells me true, though in his tale lie death, I hear him as he flatter'd.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Labienus— This is stiff news-hath, with his Parthian force, Extended Asia from Euphrates; His conquering banner shook from Syria To Lydia and to Ionia; Whilst—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Antony, thou wouldst say,—

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: O, my lord !

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Speak to me home, mince not the
general tongue: Name Cleopatra as she is call'd in Rome; Rail thou in Fulvia's phrase; and taunt my faults With such full license as both truth and malice Have power to utter. O, then we bring forth
weeds, When our quick minds lie still; and our ills
told us Is as our earing. Fare thee well awhile.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: At your noble pleasure. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
From Sicyon, ho, the news! Speak
there !

sp.speaker: First Att.
sp.p:
The man from Sicyon,— is there
such an one ?

sp.speaker: Sec. Att.
sp.p: He stays upon your will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Let him appear. These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, Or lose myself in dotage.
Enter another Messenger.
What are you ?

sp.speaker: Sec. Mess.
sp.p: Fulvia thy wife is dead.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where died she ?

sp.speaker: Sec. Mess.
sp.p:
In Sicyon: Her length of sickness, with what else more
serious Importeth thee to know, this bears.
Gives a letter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Forbear me.
Exit Sec. Messenger. There's a great spirit gone! Thus did I
desire it: What our contempt doth often hurl from us, We wish it ours again; the present pleasure, By revolution lowering, does become The opposite of itself: she's good, being gone; The hand could pluck her back that shoved
her on. I must from this enchanting queen break off: Ten thousand harms, more than the ills I know, My idleness doth hatch. How now! Enobarbus!
Re-enter ENOBARBUS.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: What's your pleasure, sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I must with haste from hence.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Why, then, we kill all our women: we see how mortal an unkindness is to them; if they suffer our departure, death's the word.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I must be gone.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Under a compelling occasion, let women die; it were pity to cast them away for nothing; though, between them and a great cause, they should be esteemed nothing. Cleo patra, catching but the least noise of this, dies instantly; I have seen her die twenty times upon far poorer moment: I do think there is mettle in death, which commits some loving act upon her, she hath such a celerity in dying.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: She is cunning past man's thought.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Alack, sir, no; her passions are made of nothing but the finest part of pure love: we cannot call her winds and waters sighs and tears; they are greater storms and tempests than almanacs can report: this cannot be cunning in her; if it be, she makes a shower of rain as well as Jove.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Would I had never seen her.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: O, sir, you had then left unseen a wonderful piece of work; which not to have been blest withal would have discredited your travel.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fulvia is dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Sir ?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fulvia is dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Fulvia!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Why, sir, give the gods a thankful sacrifice. When it pleaseth their deities to take the wife of a man from him, it shows to man the tailors of the earth; comforting therein, that when old robes are worn out, there are members to make new. If there were no more women but Fulvia, then had you indeed a cut, and the case to be lamented: this grief is crowned with consolation; your old smock brings forth a new petticoat: and indeed the tears live in an onion that should water this sorrow.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
The business she hath broached in the
state Cannot endure my absence.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: And the business you have broached here cannot be without you; especially that of Cleopatra's, which wholly depends on your abode.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
No more light answers. Let our officers Have notice what we purpose. I shall break The cause of our expedience to the queen, And get her leave to part. For not alone The death of Fulvia, with more urgent touches, Do strongly speak to us; but the letters too Of many our contriving friends in Rome Petition us at home: Sextus Pompeius Hath given the dare to Cæsar, and commands The empire of the sea: our slippery people, Whose love is never link'd to the deserver Till his deserts are past, begin to throw Pompey the Great and all his dignities Upon his son; who, high in name and power, Higher than both in blood and life, stands up For the main soldier: whose quality, going on, The sides o' the world may danger: much is
breeding, Which, like the courser's hair, hath yet but life, And not a serpent's poison. Say, our pleasure, To such whose place is under us, requires Our quick remove from hence.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I shall do't. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III
div.stage:
Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and
ALEXAS.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Where is he ?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I did not see him since.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
See where he is, who's with him, what
he does: I did not send you: if you find him sad, Say I am dancing; if in mirth, report That I am sudden sick: quick, and return.
Exit Alexas.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Madam, methinks, if you did love him
dearly, You do not hold the method to enforce The like from him.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: What should I do, I do not ?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
In each thing give him way, cross him
in nothing.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Thou teachest like a fool; the way to
lose him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Tempt him not so too far; I wish,
forbear: In time we hate that which we often fear. But here comes Antony.
Enter ANTONY.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: I am sick and sullen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
I am sorry to give breathing to my
purpose,

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Help me away, dear Charmian; I shall
fall: It cannot be thus long, the sides of nature Will not sustain it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now, my dearest queen,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Pray you, stand further from me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I know by that same eye, there's some
good news. What says the married woman ? You may go: Would she had never given you leave to come! Let her not say 'tis I that keep you here: I have no power upon you; hers you are.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: The gods best know,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: O, never was there queen So mightily betray'd! yet at the first I saw the treasons planted.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Cleopatra,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Why should I think you can be mine
and true, Though you in swearing shake the throned gods, Who have been false to Fulvia ? Riotous
madness, To be entangled with those mouth-made vows, Which break themselves in swearing!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Most sweet queen,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Nay, pray you, seek no color for your
going, But bid farewell, and go: when you sued
staying, Then was the time for words: no going then; Eternity was in our lips and eyes, Bliss in our brows' bent; none our parts so poor, But was a race of heaven: they are so still, Or thou, the greatest soldier of the world, Art turn'd the greatest liar.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How now, lady

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I would I had thy inches; thou shouldst
know There were a heart in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Hear me, queen: The strong necessity of time commands Our services awhile; but my full heart Remains in use with you. Our Italy Shines o'er with civil swords: Sextus Pompeius Makes his approaches to the port of Rome: Equality of two domestic powers Breed scrupulous faction: the hated, grown to
strength, Are newly grown to love: the condemn'd Pompey, Rich in his father's honor, creeps apace, Into the hearts of such as have not thrived Upon the present state, whose numbers threaten; And quietness, grown sick of rest, would purge By any desperate change: my more particular, And that which most with you should safe my
going, Is Fulvia's death.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Though age from folly could not give
me freedom, It does from childishness: can Fulvia die ?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: She's dead, my queen: Look here, and at thy sovereign leisure read The garboils she awaked; at the last, best: See when and where she died.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: O most false love! Where be the sacred vials thou shouldst fill With sorrowful water ? Now I see, I see, In Fulvia's death, how mine received shall be.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Quarrel no more, but be prepared to
know The purposes I bear; which are, or cease, As you shall give the advice. By the fire That quickens Nilus' slime, I go from hence Thy soldier, servant; making peace or war As thou affect'st.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Cut my lace, Charmian, come; But let it be: I am quickly ill, and well, So Antony loves.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My precious queen, forbear; And give true evidence to his love, which stands An honorable trial.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: So Fulvia told me. I prithee, turn aside and weep for her, Then bid adieu to me, and say the tears Belong to Egypt: good now, play one scene Of excellent dissembling; and let it look Life perfect honor.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You'll heat my blood: no more.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
You can do better yet; but this is
meetly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now, by my sword,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
And target. Still he mends; But this is not the best. Look, prithee,
Charmian, How this Herculean Roman does become The carriage of his chafe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I'll leave you, lady.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Courteous lord, one word. Sir, you and I must part, but that's not it: Sir, you and I have loved, but there's not it; That you know well: something it is I would, O, my oblivion is a very Antony, And I am all forgotten.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: But that your royalty Holds idleness your subject, I should take you For idleness itself.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: 'Tis sweating labor To bear such idleness so near the heart As Cleopatra this. But, sir, forgive me; Since my becomings kill me, when they do not Eye well to you: your honor calls you hence; Therefore be deaf to my unpitied folly. And all the gods go with you! upon your sword Sit laurel victory ! and smooth success Be strew'd before your feet!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Let us go. Come; Our separation so abides, and flies, That thou, residing here, go'st yet with me, And I, hence fleeting, here remain with thee. Away! Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV
div.stage:
Enter OCTAVIUS CÆSAR, reading a letter,
LEPIDUS, and their Train.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
You may see, Lepidus, and henceforth
know, It is not Cæsar's natural vice to hate Our great competitor: from Alexandria This is the news: he fishes, drinks, and wastes The lamps of night in revel; is not more manlike Than Cleopatra; nor the queen of Ptolemy More womanly than he; hardly gave audience, or Vouchsafed to think he had partners: you shall
find there A man who is the abstract of all faults That all men follow.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: I must not think there are Evils enow to darken all his goodness: His faults in him seem as the spots of heaven, More fiery by night's blackness; hereditary, Rather than purchased; what he cannot change, Than what he chooses.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
You are too indulgent. Let us grant, it
is not Amiss to tumble on the bed of Ptolemy; To give a kingdom for a mirth; to sit And keep the turn of tippling with a slave; To reel the streets at noon, and stand the buffet With knaves that smell of sweat: say this becomes
him,— As his composure must be rare indeed Whom these things cannot blemish,—yet must
Antony No way excuse his soils, when we do bear So great weight in his lightness. If he fill'd His vacancy with his voluptuousness, Full surfeits, and the dryness of his bones, Call on him for't: but to confound such time, That drums him from his sport, and speaks as
loud As his own state and ours,—'tis to be chid As we rate boys, who, being mature in
knowledge, Pawn their experience to their present pleasure, And so rebel to judgment.
Enter a Messenger.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Here's more news.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Thy biddings have been done; and
every hour, Most noble Cæsar, shalt thou have report How 'tis abroad. Pompey is strong at sea; And it appears he is beloved of those That only have fear'd Cæsar: to the ports The discontents repair, and men's reports Give him much wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
I should have known no less. It hath been taught us from the primal state, That he which is was wish'd until he were; And the ebb'd man, ne'er loved till ne'er worth
love, Comes dear'd by being lack'd. This common
body, Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream, Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide, To rot itself with motion.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Cæsar, I bring thee word, Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates, Make the sea serve them, which they ear and
wound With keels of every kind: many hot inroads They make in Italy; the borders maritime Lack blood to think on 't, and flush youth revolt: No vessel can peep forth, but 'tis as soon Taken as seen; for Pompey's name strikes more Than could his war resisted.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
Antony, Leave thy lascivious wassails. When thou once Wast beaten from Modena, where thou slew'st Hirtius and Pansa, consuls, at thy heel Did famine follow; whom thou fought'st against, Though daintily brought up, with patience more Than savages could suffer: thou didst drink The stale of horses, and the gilded puddle Which beasts would cough at: thy palate then
did deign The roughest berry on the rudest hedge; Yea, like the stag, when snow the pasture sheets, The barks of trees thou browsed'st; on the Alps It is reported thou didst eat strange flesh, Which some did die to look on: and all this- It wounds thine honor that I speak it now— Was borne so like a soldier, that thy cheek So much as lank'd not.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis pity of him.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Let his shames quickly Drive him to Rome: 'tis time we twain Did show ourselves i' the field; and to that end Assemble we immediate council: Pompey Thrives in our idleness.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: To-morrow, Cæsar, I shall be furnish'd to inform you rightly Both what by sea and land I can be able To front this present time.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Till which encounter, It is my business too. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Farewell, my lord: what you shall know
meantime Of stirs abroad, I shall beseech you, sir, To let me be partaker.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Doubt not, sir; I knew it for my bond. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V
div.stage:
Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and
MARDIAN.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Charmian!

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Madam ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Ha, ha! Give me to drink mandragora.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Why, madam ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
That I might sleep out this great gap of
time My Antony is away.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You think of him too much.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: O, 'tis treason !

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Madam, I trust, not so.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Thou, eunuch Mardian!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What's your highness' pleasure ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Not now to hear thee sing; I take no
pleasure In aught an eunuch has: 'tis well for thee, That, being unseminar'd, thy freer thoughts May not fly forth of Egypt. Hast thou affections ?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes, gracious madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Indeed !

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p:
Not in deed, madam; for I can do
nothing But what indeed is honest to be done: Yet have I fierce affections, and think What Venus did with Mars.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
O Charmian, Where think'st thou he is now ? Stands he, or
sits he ? Or does he walk ? or is he on his horse ? O happy horse, to bear the weight of Antony ! Do bravely, horse ! for wot'st thou whom thou
movest ? The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm And burgonet of men. He's speaking now, Or murmuring 'Where's my serpent of old
Nile ?' For so he calls me: now I feed myself With most delicious poison. Think on me, That am with Phoebus' amorous pinches black, And wrinkled deep in time ? Broad-fronted Cæsar, When thou wast here above the ground, I was A morsel for a monarch: and great Pompey Would stand and make his eyes grow in my
brow; There would he anchor his aspect and die With looking on his life.
Enter ALEXAS, from CÆSAR.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Sovereign of Egypt, hail !

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: How much unlike art thou Mark Antony ! Yet, coming from him, that great medicine hath With his tinct gilded thee. How goes it with my brave Mark Antony ?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Last thing he did, dear queen, He kiss'd,—the last of many doubled kisses,— This orient pearl. His speech sticks in my heart.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Mine ear must pluck it thence.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p:
'Good friend,' quoth he, 'Say, the firm Roman to great Egypt sends This treasure of an oyster; at whose foot, To mend the petty present, I will piece Her opulent throne with kingdoms; all the east, Say thou, shall call her mistress.' So he nodded, And soberly did mount an arm-gaunt steed, Who neigh'd so high, that what I would have
spoke Was beastly dumb'd by him.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: What, was he sad or merry ?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p:
Like to the time o' the year between
the extremes Of hot and cold, he was nor sad nor merry.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
O well-divided disposition! Note him, Note him, good Charmian, 'tis the man; but
note him: He was not sad, for he would shine on those That make their looks by his; he was not merry, Which seem'd to tell them his remembrance lay In Egypt with his joy; but between both: O heavenly mingle! Be'st thou sad or merry, The violence of either thee becomes, So does it no man else. Met'st thou my posts ?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Ay, madam, twenty several messengers: Why do you send so thick ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Who's born that day When I forget to send to Antony, Shall die a beggar. Ink and paper, Charmian. Welcome, my good Alexas. Did I, Charmian, Ever love Cæsar so ?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: O that brave Cæsar !

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Be choked with such another emphasis ! Say, the brave Antony.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: The valiant Cæsar !

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: By Isis, I will give thee bloody teeth, If thou with Cæsar paragon again My man of men.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: By your most gracious pardon, I sing but after you.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: My salad days, When I was green in judgment: cold in blood, To say as I said then! But, come, away; Get me ink and paper: He shall have every day a several greeting, Or I'll unpeople Egypt. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter POMPEY, MENECRATES, and MENAS,
in warlike manner.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
If the great gods be just, they shall
assist The deeds of justest men.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: Know, worthy Pompey, That what they do delay, they not deny.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Whiles we are suitors to their throne,
decays The thing we sue for.

sp.speaker: Mene.
Pom.
sp.p: I shall do well: The people love me, and the sea is mine; My powers are crescent, and my auguring hope Says it will come to the full. Mark Antony In Egypt sits at dinner, and will make No wars without doors: Cæsar gets money where He loses hearts: Lepidus flatters both, Of both is flatter'd; but he neither loves, Nor either cares for him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Cæsar and Lepidus Are in the field: a mighty strength they carry.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Where have you this ? 'tis false.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: From Silvius, sir.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
He dreams: I know they are in Rome
together, Looking for Antony. But all the charms of love, Salt Cleopatra, soften thy waned lip! Let witchcraft join with beauty, lust with both ! Tie up the libertine in a field of feasts, Keep his brain fuming; Epicurean cooks Sharpen with cloyless sauce his appetite; That sleep and feeding may prorogue his honor Even till a Lethe'd dulness!
Enter VARRIUS.
How now, Varrius!

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.p: This is most certain that I shall deliver: Mark Antony is every hour in Rome Expected: since he went from Egypt 'tis A space for further travel.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
I could have given less matter A better ear. Menas, I did not think This amorous surfeiter would have donn'd his
helm For such a petty war: his soldiership Is twice the other twain: but let us rear The higher our opinion, that our stirring Can from the lap of Egypt's widow pluck The ne'er-lust-wearied Antony.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I cannot hope Cæsar and Antony shall well greet together: His wife that's dead did trespasses to Cæsar; His brother warr'd upon him; although, I think, Not moved by Antony.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
I know not, Menas, How lesser enmities may give way to greater. Were't not that we stand up against them all, 'Twere pregnant they should square between
themselves; For they have entertained cause enough To draw their swords: but how the fear of us May cement their divisions and bind up The petty difference, we yet not know. Be't as our gods will have't! It only stands Our lives upon to use our strongest hands. Come, Menas. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Good Enobarbus, 'tis a worthy deed, And shall become you well, to entreat your
captain To soft and gentle speech.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I shall entreat him To answer like himself: if Cæsar move him, Let Antony look over Cæsar's head And speak as loud as Mars. By Jupiter, Were I the wearer of Antonius' beard, I would not shave't to-day.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis not a time For private stomaching.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Every time Serves for the matter that is then born in't.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
But small to greater matters must give
way.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Not if the small come first.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Your speech is passion: But, pray you, stir no embers up. Here comes The noble Antony.
Enter ANTONY and VENTIDUS.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
And yonder, Cæsar.
Enter CÆSAR, MECÆNAS, and AGRIPPA.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If we compose well here, to Parthia: Hark, Ventidius.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: I do not know, Mecænas; ask Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Noble friends, That which combined us was most great, and let
not A leaner action rend us. What's amiss, May it be gently heard: when we debate Our trivial difference loud, we do commit Murder in healing wounds: then, noble partners, The rather, for I earnestly beseech, Touch you the sourest points with sweetest terms, Nor curstness grow to the matter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: 'Tis spoken well. Were we before our armies, and to fight. I should do thus. Flourish.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Welcome to Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Sit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Sit, sir.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Nay, then.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
I learn, you take things ill which are
not so, Or being, concern you not.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
I must be laugh'd at, If, or for nothing or a little, I Should say myself offended, and with you Chiefly i' the world; more laugh'd at, that I
should Once name you derogately, when to sound your
name It not concern'd me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My being in Egypt, Cæsar, What was't to you ?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: No more than my residing here at Rome Might be to you in Egypt: yet, if you there Did practise on my state, your being in Egypt Might be my question.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How intend you, practised ?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
You may be pleased to catch at mine
intent By what did here befal me. Your wife and
brother Made wars upon me; and their contestation Was theme for you, you were the word of war.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
You do mistake your business; my
brother never Did urge me in his act: I did inquire it; And have my learning from some true reports, That drew their swords with you. Did he not
rather Discredit my authority with yours; And make the wars alike against my stomach, Having alike your cause ? Of this my letters Before did satisfy you. If you'll patch a quarrel, As matter whole you have not to make it with, It must not be with this.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: You praise yourself By laying defects of judgment to me; but You patch'd up your excuses.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Not so, not so; I know you could not lack, I am certain on't, Very necessity of this thought, that I, Your partner in the cause 'gainst which he fought, Could not with graceful eyes attend those wars Which fronted mine own peace. As for my wife, I would you had her spirit in such another: The third o' the world is yours; which with a
snaffle You may pace easy, but not such a wife.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Would we had all such wives, that the men might go to wars with the women!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
So much uncurbable, her garboils,
Cæsar, Made out of her impatience, which not wanted Shrewdness of policy too, I grieving grant Did you too much disquiet: for that you must But say, I could not help it.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: I wrote to you When rioting in Alexandria; you Did pocket up my letters, and with taunts Did gibe my missive out of audience.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Sir, He fell upon me ere admitted: then Three kings I had newly feasted, and did want Of what I was i' the morning: but next day I told him of myself; which was as much As to have ask'd him pardon. Let this fellow Be nothing of our strife; if we contend, Out of our question wipe him.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: You have broken The article of your oath; which you shall never Have tongue to charge me with.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Soft, Cæsar !

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No, Lepidus, let him speak: The honor is sacred which he talks on now, Supposing that I lack'd it. But, on, Cæsar; The article of my oath.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
To lend me arms and aid when I required
them; The which you both denied.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Neglected, rather; And then when poison'd hours had bound me up >From mine own knowledge. As nearly as I may, I'll play the penitent to you: but mine honesty Shall not make poor my greatness, nor my power Work without it. Truth is, that Fulvia, To have me out of Egypt, made wars here; For which myself, the ignorant motive, do So far ask pardon as befits mine honor To stoop in such a case.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis noble spoken.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p:
If it might please you, to enforce no
further The griefs between ye: to forget them quite Were to remember that the present need Speaks to atone you.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Worthily spoken, Mecænas.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Or, if you borrow one another's love for the instant, you may, when you hear no more words of Pompey, return it again: you shall have time to wrangle in when you have nothing else to do.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thou art a soldier only: speak no more.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: That truth should be silent I had almost forgot.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
You wrong this presence; therefore
speak no more.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Go to, then; your considerate stone.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
I do not much dislike the matter, but The manner of his speech; for't cannot be We shall remain in friendship, our conditions So differing in their acts. Yet, if I knew What hoop should hold us stanch, from edge to
edge O' the world I would pursue it.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Give me leave, Cæsar,—

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Speak, Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Thou hast a sister by the mother's side, Admired Octavia: great Mark Antony Is now a widower.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Say not so, Agrippa: If Cleopatra heard you, your reproof Were well deserved of rashness.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I am not married, Cæsar: let me hear Agrippa further speak.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p:
To hold you in perpetual amity, To make you brothers, and to knit your hearts With an unslipping knot, take Antony Octavia to his wife; whose beauty claims No worse a husband than the best of men; Whose virtue and whose general graces speak That which none else can utter. By this
marriage, All little jealousies, which now seem great, And all great fears, which now import their
dangers, Would then be nothing: truths would be tales, Where now half tales be truths: her love to both Would, each to other and all loves to both, Draw after her. Pardon what I have spoke; For 'tis a studied, not a present thought, By duty ruminated.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Will Cæsar speak?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Not till he hears how Antony is touch'd With what is spoke already.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What power is in Agrippa, If I would say, 'Agrippa, be it so,' To make this good ?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: The power of Cæsar, and His power unto Octavia.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: May I never To this good purpose, that so fairly shows, Dream of impediment ! Let me have thy hand : Further this act of grace: and from this hour The heart of brothers govern in our loves And sway our great designs!

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: There is my hand. A sister I bequeath you, whom no brother Did ever love so dearly: let her live To join our kingdoms and our hearts; and never Fly off our loves again!

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Happily, amen!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
I did not think to draw my sword
'gainst Pompey; For he hath laid strange courtesies and great Of late upon me: I must thank him only, Lest my remembrance suffer ill report; At heel of that, defy him.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Time calls upon's: Of us must Pompey presently be sought, Or else he seeks out us.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where lies he?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: About the mount Misenum.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What is his strength by land?

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Great and increasing: but by sea He is an absolute master.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: So is the fame. Would we had spoke together! Haste we for it: Yet, ere we put ourselves in arms, dispatch we The business we have talk'd of.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: With most gladness: And do invite you to my sister's view, Whither straight I'll lead you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Let us, Lepidus, Not lack your company.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Noble Antony, Not sickness should detain me.
Flourish. Exeunt Cæsar, Antony,
and Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Welcome from Egypt, sir.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Half the heart of Cæsar, worthy Mecænas! My honorable friend, Agrippa !

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Good Enobarbus!

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: We have cause to be glad that matters are so well digested. You stayed well by 't in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Ay, sir; we did sleep day out of countenance, and made the night light with drinking.

sp.speaker: Mec.
Eno.
sp.p: This was but as a fly by an eagle: we had much more monstrous matter of feast, which worthily deserved noting.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: She's a most triumphant lady, if report be square to her.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: When she first met Mark Antony, she pursed up his heart, upon the river of Cydnus.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: There she appeared indeed; or my reporter devised well for her.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
I will tell you. The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne, Burn'd on the water: the poop was beaten gold; Purple the sails, and so perfumed that The winds were love-sick with them; the oars
were silver, Which to the tune of flutes kept stroke, and made The water which they beat to follow faster, As amorous of their strokes. For her own person, It beggar'd all description: she did lie In her pavilion—cloth-of-gold of tissue— O'er-picturing that Venus where we see The fancy outwork nature: on each side her Stood pretty dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids, With divers-color'd fans, whose wind did seem To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool, And what they undid did.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: O, rare for Antony!

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Her gentlewomen, like the Nereides, So many mermaids, tended her i' the eyes, And made their bends adornings: at the helm A seeming mermaid steers: the silken tackle Swell with the touches of those flower-soft hands, That yarely frame the office. From the barge A strange invisible perfume hits the sense Of the adjacent wharfs. The city cast Her people out upon her; and Antony, Enthroned i' the market-place, did sit alone, Whistling to the air; which, but for vacancy, Had gone to gaze on Cleopatra too, And made a gap in nature.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Rare Egyptian!

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Upon her landing, Antony sent to her, Invited her to supper: she replied, It should be better he became her guest; Which she entreated: our courteous Antony, Whom ne'er the word of 'No' woman heard
speak, Being barber'd ten times o'er, goes to the feast, And for his ordinary pays his heart For what his eyes eat only.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Royal wench! She made great Cæsar lay his sword to bed: He plough'd her, and she cropp'd.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I saw her once Hop forty paces through the public street; And having lost her breath, she spoke, and panted, That she did make defect perfection, And, breathless, power breathe forth.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Now Antony must leave her utterly.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Never; he will not: Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale Her infinite variety: other women cloy The appetites they feed: but she makes hungry Where most she satisfies; for vilest things Become themselves in her: that the holy priests Bless her when she is riggish.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: If beauty, wisdom, modesty, can settle The heart of Antony, Octavia is A blessed lottery to him.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Let us go. Good Enobarbus, make yourself my guest Whilst you abide here.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Humbly, sir, I thank you. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III
div.stage:
Enter ANTONY, CÆSAR, OCTAVIA between them,
and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
The world and my great office will
sometimes Divide me from your bosom.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: All which time Before the gods my knee shall bow my prayers To them for you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Good night, sir. My Octavia, Read not my blemishes in the world's report: I have not kept my square;
                                          but that to come Shall
                                          all be done by the rule. Good night, dear 
lady. Good night, sir.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
Good night.
Exeunt Cæsar and Octavia.
Enter Soothsayer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Now, sirrah; you do wish yourself in
Egypt ?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p:
Would I had never come from thence,
nor you Thither!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If you can, your reason ?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: I see it in My motion, have it not in my tongue : but yet Hie you to Egypt again.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Say to me, Whose fortunes shall rise higher, Cæsar's or mine ?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Cæsar's. Therefore, O Antony, stay not by his side: Thy demon, that's thy spirit which keeps thee, is Noble, courageous, high, unmatchable, Where Cæsar's is not; but, near him, thy angel Becomes a fear, as being o'erpower'd: therefore Make space enough between you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Speak this no more.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p:
To none but thee; no more, but when
to thee. If thou dost play with him at any game, Thou art sure to lose; and, of that natural luck, He beats thee 'gainst the odds: thy lustre
thickens, When he shines by: I say again, thy spirit Is all afraid to govern thee near him; But, he away, 'tis noble.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Get thee gone: Say to Ventidius I would speak with him:
Exit Soothsayer. He shall to Parthia. Be it art or hap, He hath spoken true : the very dice obey him; And in our sports my better cunning faints Under his chance : if we draw lots, he speeds; His cocks do win the battle still of mine, When it is all to nought; and his quails ever Beat mine, inhoop'd, at odds. I will to Egypt: And though I make this marriage for my peace, I' the east my pleasure lies.
Enter VENTIDIUS.
O, come, Ventidius, You must to Parthia: your commission's ready; Follow me, and receive't.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Trouble yourselves no further: pray you,
hasten Your generals after.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Sir, Mark Antony Will e'en but kiss Octavia, and we'll follow.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p:
Till I shall see you in your soldier's
dress, Which will become you both, farewell.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: We shall, As I conceive the journey, be at the Mount Before you, Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Your way is shorter; My purposes do draw me much about: You'll win two days upon me.

sp.speaker: Mec., Agr.
sp.p: Sir, good success !

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Farewell. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V
div.stage:
Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and
ALEXAS.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Give me some music; music, moody food Of us that trade in love.

sp.speaker: Att.
sp.p:
The music, ho !
Enter MARDIAN the Eunuch.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Let it alone; let's to billiards: come,
Charmian.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: My arm is sore; best play with Mardian.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
As well a woman with an eunuch play'd As with a woman. Come, you'll play with me,
sir ?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: As well as I can, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
And when good will is show'd, though't
come too short, The actor may plead pardon. I'll none now: Give me mine angle; we'll to the river: there, My music playing far off, I will betray Tawny-finn'd fishes; my bended hook shall pierce Their slimy jaws; and, as I draw them up, I'll think them every one an Antony, And say 'Ah, ha! you're caught.'

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Twas merry when You wager'd on your angling; when your diver Did hang a salt-fish on his hook, which he With fervency drew up.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
That time,—O times!— I laugh'd him out of patience; and that night I laugh'd him into patience; and next morn, Ere the ninth hour, I drunk him to his bed; Then put my tires and mantles on him, whilst I wore his sword Philippan.
Enter a Messenger.
O, from Italy Ram thou thy fruitful tidings in mine ears, That long time have been barren.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Madam, madam,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Antonius dead !— If thou say so, villain, Thou kill'st thy mistress: but well and free, If thou so yield him, there is gold, and here My bluest veins to kiss; a hand that kings Have lipp'd, and trembled kissing.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: First, madam, he is well.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Why, there's more gold. But, sirrah, mark, we use To say the dead are well: bring it to that, The gold I give thee will I melt and pour Down thy ill-uttering throat.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Good madam, hear me.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Well, go to, I will; But there's no goodness in thy face: if Antony Be free and healthful,—so tart a favor To trumpet such good tidings! If not well, Thou shouldst come like a Fury crown'd with
snakes, Not like a formal man.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Will't please you hear me ?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I have a mind to strike thee ere thou
speak'st: Yet, if thou say Antony lives, is well, Or friends with Cæsar, or not captive to him, I'll set thee in a shower of gold, and hail Rich pearls upon thee.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Madam, he's well.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Well said.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: And friends with Cæsar.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Thou'rt an honest man.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Cæsar and he are greater friends than
ever.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Make thee a fortune from me.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: But yet, madam—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I do not like 'But yet,' it does allay The good precedence; fie upon 'But yet'! 'But yet' is as a gaoler to bring forth Some monstrous malefactor. Prithee, friend, Pour out the pack of matter to mine ear, The good and bad together: he's friends with
Cæsar: In state of health thou say'st; and thou say'st
free.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Free, madam! no; I made no such
report: He's bound unto Octavia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: For what good turn?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: For the best turn i' the bed.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: I am pale, Charmian.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Madam, he's married to Octavia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
The most infectious pestilence upon
thee! Strikes him down.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Good madam, patience.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
What say you ? Hence,
Strikes him again. Horrible villain! or I'll spurn thine eyes Like balls before me; I'll unhair thy head:
She hales him up and down. Thou shalt be whipp'd with wire, and stew'd in
brine, Smarting in lingering pickle.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Gracious madam, I that do bring the news made not the match.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Say 'tis not so, a province I will give
thee, And make thy fortunes proud: the blow thou
hadst Shall make thy peace for moving me to rage; And I will boot thee with what gift beside Thy modesty can beg.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: He's married, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Rogue, thou hast lived too long.
Draws a knife.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Nay, then I'll run. What mean you, madam? I have made no fault. Exit.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Good madam, keep yourself within
yourself : The man is innocent.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Some innocents 'scape not the thunderbolt. Melt Egypt into Nile! and kindly creatures Turn all to serpents! Call the slave again: Though I am mad, I will not bite him: call.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: He is afeard to come.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I will not hurt him.
Exit Charmian. These hands do lack nobility, that they strike A meaner than myself; since I myself Have given myself the cause.
Re-enter CHARMIAN and Messenger.
Come hither, sir. Though it be honest, it is never good To bring bad news: give to a gracious message. An host of tongues; but let ill tidings tell Themselves when they be felt.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: I have done my duty.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Is he married ? I cannot hate thee worser than I do, If thou again say 'Yes.'

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: He's married, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
The gods confound thee! dost thou hold
there still ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Should I lie, madam?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: O, I would thou didst, So half my Egypt were submerged and made A cistern for scaled snakes! Go, get thee hence: Hadst thou Narcissus in thy face, to me Thou wouldst appear most ugly. He is married ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: I crave your highness' pardon. n=98

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: He is married ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Take no offence that I would not offend
you: To punish me for what you make me do. Seems much unequal: he's married to Octavia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
O, that his fault should make a knave
of thee, That art not what thou'rt sure of! Get thee hence: The merchandise which thou hast brought from
Rome Are all too dear for me: lie they upon thy hand, And be undone by 'em! Exit Messenger.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good your highness, patience.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
In praising Antony, I have dispraised
Cæsar.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Many times, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I am paid for't now. Lead me from hence: I faint: O Iras, Charmian ! 'tis no matter. Go to the fellow, good Alexas; bid him Report the feature of Octavia, her years, Her inclination, let him not leave out The color of her hair: bring me word quickly.
Exit Alexas. Let him for ever go :—let him not—Charmian, Though he be painted one way like a Gorgon, The other way's a Mars. Bid you Alexas
To Mardian. Bring me word how tall she is. Pity me,
Charmian, But do not speak to me. Lead me to my chamber. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VI
div.stage:
Flourish. Enter POMPEY and MENAS at one
door, with drum and trumpet: at another,
CÆSAR, ANTONY, LEPIDUS, ENOBARBUS,
MECÆNAS, with Soldiers marching.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Your hostages I have, so have you
mine; And we shall talk before we fight.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Most meet That first we come to words; and therefore have we Our written purposes before us sent; Which, if thou hast consider'd, let us know If 'twill tie up thy discontented sword, And carry back to Sicily much tall youth That else must perish here.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
To you all three, The senators alone of this great world, Chief factors for the gods, I do not know Wherefore my father should revengers want, Having a son and friends; since Julius Cæsar, Who at Philippi the good Brutus ghosted, There saw you laboring for him. What was't That moved pale Cassius to conspire; and what Made the all-honor'd, honest Roman, Brutus, With the arm'd rest, courtiers and beauteous
freedom, To drench the Capitol; but that they would Have one man but a man ? And that is it Hath made me rig my navy; at whose burthen The anger'd ocean foams; with which I meant To scourge the ingratitude that despiteful Rome Cast on my noble father.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Take your time.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Thou canst not fear us, Pompey, with
thy sails; We'll speak with thee at sea: at land, thou
know'st How much we do o'er-count thee.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: At land, indeed, Thou dost o'er-count me of my father's house : But, since the cuckoo builds not for himself, Remain in't as thou mayst.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Be pleased to tell us— For this is from the present—how you take The offers we have sent you.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: There's the point.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Which do not be entreated to, but weigh What it is worth embraced.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: And what may follow, To try a larger fortune.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: You have made me offer Of Sicily, Sardinia; and I must Rid all the sea of pirates; then, to send Measures of wheat to Rome; this 'greed upon To part with unhack'd edges, and bear back Our targes undinted.

sp.speaker: Cæs. Ant. Lep.
sp.p: That's our offer.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Know, then, I came before you here a man prepared To take this offer: but Mark Antony Put me to some impatience: though I lose The praise of it by telling, you must know, When Cæsar and your brother were at blows, Your mother came to Sicily and did find Her welcome friendly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I have heard it, Pompey; And am well studied for a liberal thanks Which I do owe you.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Let me have your hand: I did not think, sir, to have met you here.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
The beds i' the east are soft; and thanks
to you, That call'd me timelier than my purpose hither; For I have gain'd by 't.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Since I saw you last, There is a change upon you.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Well, I know not What counts harsh fortune casts upon my face; But in my bosom shall she never come, To make my heart her vassal.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Well met here.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
I hope so, Lepidus. Thus we are
agreed: I crave our composition may be written, And seal'd between us.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: That's the next to do.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
We'll feast each other ere we part;
and let's Draw lots who shall begin.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: That will I, Pompey.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
No, Antony, take the lot: but, first Or last, your fine Egyptian cookery Shall have the fame. I have heard that Julius
Cæsar Grew fat with feasting there.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You have heard much.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: I have fair meanings, sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And fair words to them.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Then so much have I heard: And I have heard, Apollodorus carried-

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: No more of that: he did so.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: What, I pray you ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: A certain queen to Cæsar in a mattress.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
I know thee now: how farest thou,
soldier ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Well; And well am like to do; for, I perceive, Four feasts are toward.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Let me shake thy hand; I never hated thee: I have seen thee fight, When I have envied thy behavior.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Sir, I never loved you much; but I ha' praised ye, When you have well deserved ten times as much As I have said you did.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Enjoy thy plainness, It nothing ill becomes thee. Aboard my galley I invite you all: Will you lead, lords ?

sp.speaker: Cæs. Ant. Lep.
sp.p: Show us the way, sir.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Come.
Exeunt all but Menas and Enobarbus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Thy father, Pompey, would ne'er have made this treaty.—You and I have known, sir.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: At sea, I think.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: We have, sir.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: You have done well by water.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: And you by land.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I will praise any man that will praise me; though it cannot be denied what I have done by land.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Nor what I have done by water.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Yes, something you can deny for your own safety: you have been a great thief by sea.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: And you by land.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: There I deny my land service. But give me your hand, Menas: if our eyes had authority, here they might take two thieves kissing.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: All men's faces are true, what- some'er their hands are.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: But there is never a fair woman has a true face.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: No slander; they steal hearts.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: We came hither to fight with you.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: For my part, I am sorry it is turned to a drinking. Pompey doth this day laugh away his fortune.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: If he do, sure, he cannot weep't back again.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: You've said, sir. We looked not for Mark Antony here: pray you, is he married to Cleopatra?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Cæsar's sister is called Octavia.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: True, sir; she was the wife of Caius Marcellus.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: But she is now the wife of Marcus Antonius.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Pray ye, sir?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: 'Tis true.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Then is Cæsar and he for ever knit together.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: If I were bound to divine of this unity, I would not prophesy so.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I think the policy of that purpose made more in the marriage than the love of the parties.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I think so too. But you shall find, the band that seems to tie their friendship together will be the very strangler of their amity: Octavia is of a holy, cold, and still conversation.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Who would not have his wife so ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Not he that himself is not so; which is Mark Antony. He will to his Egyptian dish again: then shall the sighs of Octavia blow the fire up in Cæsar; and, as I said before, that which is the strength of their amity shall prove the immediate author of their variance. Antony will use his affection where it is: he married but his occasion here.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: And thus it may be. Come, sir, will you aboard ? I have a health for you.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: I shall take it, sir: we have used our throats in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Come, let's away. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VII
div.stage:
On board Pompey's galley, off
Misenum.

Enter two or three Servants with
a banquet.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: Here they'll be, man. Some o' their plants are ill-rooted already; the least wind i' the world will blow them down.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Lepidus is high-colored.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: They have made him drink alms-drink.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: As they pinch one another by the disposition, he cries out 'No more;' reconciles them to his entreaty, and himself to the drink.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p: But it raises the greater war between him and his discretion.

sp.speaker: Sec. Serv.
sp.p: Why, this is to have a name in great men's fellowship: I had as lief have a reed that will do me no service as a partisan I could not heave.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.p:
To be called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in't, are the holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disaster the cheeks.
A sennet sounded. Enter CÆSAR,
ANTONY,LEPIDUS, POMPEY, AGRIPPA, MECÆNAS,
ENOBARBUS, MENAS, with other captains.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Thus do they, sir: they take
the flow o' the Nile By certain scales i' the pyramid; they know, By the height, the lowness, or the mean, if dearth Or foison follow: the higher Nilus swells, The more it promises: as it ebbs, the seedsman Upon the slime and ooze scatters his grain, And shortly comes to harvest.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: You've strange serpents there.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ay, Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Your serpent of Egypt is bred now of your mud by the operation of your sun: so is your crocodile.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: They are so.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Sit,—and some wine! A health to Lepidus!

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: I am not so well as I should be, but I'll ne'er out.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Not till you have slept; I fear me you'll be in till then.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Nay, certainly, I have heard the Ptolemies' pyramises are very goodly things; without contradiction, I have heard that.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Pompey, a word.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Say in
mine ear: what is't ?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
Forsake thy seat, I do
beseech thee, captain, And hear me speak a word.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Forbear me till anon.
This wine for Lepidus!

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: What manner o' thing is your crocodile ?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: It is shaped, sir, like itself; and it is as broad as it hath breadth: it is just so high as it is, and moves with its own organs: it lives by that which nourisheth it; and the elements once out of it, it transmigrates.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: What color is it of?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Of it own color too.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis a strange serpent.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: 'Tis so. And the tears of it are wet.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Will this description satisfy him ?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: With the health that Pompey gives him, else he is a very epicure.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Go hang, sir, hang!
Tell me of that? away! Do as I bid you. Where's this cup I call'd for ?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
If for the sake of merit
thou wilt hear me, Rise from thy stool.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
I think thou'rt mad.
The matter ? Rises, and walks aside.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
I have ever held my cap off to thy
fortunes.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Thou hast served me with much faith.
What's else to say ? Be jolly, lords.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: These quick-sands, Lepidus, Keep off them, for you sink.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Wilt thou be lord of all the world ?

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: What say'st thou ?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
Wilt thou be lord of the whole world ?
That's twice.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: How should that be ?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: But entertain it, And, though thou think me poor, I am the man Will give thee all the world.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Hast thou drunk well?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
Now, Pompey, I have kept me from the
cup. Thou art, if thou darest be, the earthly Jove: Whate'er the ocean pales, or sky inclips, Is thine, if thou wilt ha't.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Show me which way.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
These three world-sharers, these
competitors, Are in thy vessel: let me cut the cable; And, when we are put off, fall to their throats: All there is thine.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
Ah, this thou shouldst have done, And not have spoke on't! In me 'tis villany; In thee't had been good service. Thou must
know, 'Tis not my profit that does lead mine honor; Mine honor, it. Repent that e'er thy tongue Hath so betray'd thine act: being done unknown, I should have found it afterwards well done; But must condemn it now. Desist, and drink.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
For this, I'll never follow thy pall'd fortunes more. Who seeks, and will not take when once 'tis
offer'd, Shall never find it more.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: This health to Lepidus!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Bear him ashore. I'll pledge it for him,
Pompey.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Here's to thee, Menas!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Enobarbus, welcome!

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Fill till the cup be hid.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
There's a strong fellow, Menas.
Pointing to the Attendant who carries
off Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Why ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: A' bears the third part of the world, man; see'st not?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
The third part, then, is drunk: would
it were all, That it might go on wheels!

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Drink thou; increase the reels.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Come.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: This is not yet an Alexandrian feast.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
It ripens towards it. Strike the vessels,
ho ? Here is to Cæsar!

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: I could well forbear 't. It's monstrous labor, when I wash my brain, And it grows fouler.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Be a child o' the time.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Possess it, I'll make answer: But I had rather fast from all four days Than drink so much in one.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Ha, my brave emperor! To Antony. Shall we dance now the Egyptian Bacchanals, And celebrate our drink ?

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Let's ha't, good soldier.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Come, let's all take hands, Till that the conquering wine hath steep'd our
sense In soft and delicate Lethe.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
All take hands. Make battery to our ears with the loud music: The while I'll place you: then the boy shall sing; The holding every man shall bear as loud As his strong sides can volley.
Music plays. Enobarbus places them
hand in hand. THE SONG. Come, thou monarch of the vine, Plumpy Bacchus with pink eyne! In thy fats our cares be drown'd, With thy grapes our hairs be crown'd: Cup us, till the world go round, Cup us, till the world go round!

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
What would you more? Pompey, good
night. Good brother, Let me request you off: our graver business Frowns at this levity. Gentle lords, let's part; You see we have burnt our cheeks: strong
Enobarb Is weaker than the wine; and mine own tongue Splits what it speaks: the wild disguise hath
almost Antick'd us all. What needs more words ? Good
night. Good Antony, your hand.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: I'll try you on the shore.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And shall, sir; give's your hand.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p:
O Antony, You have my father's house,--But, what ? we are
friends. Come, down into the boat.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Take heed you fall not.
Exeunt all but Enobarbus and Menas. Menas, I'll not on shore.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p:
No, to my cabin. These drums! these trumpets, flutes! what! Let Neptune hear we bid a loud farewell To these great fellows: sound and be hang'd,
sound out! Sound a flourish, with drums.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Ho ! says a'. There's my cap.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Ho! Noble captain, come. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter VENTIDIUS as it were in triumph, with
SILIUS, and other Romans, Officers, and
Soldiers; the dead body of PACORUS borne before
him.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p:
Now, darting Parthia, art thou struck;
and now Pleased fortune does of Marcus Crassus' death Make me revenger. Bear the king's son's body Before our army. Thy Pacorus, Orodes, Pays this for Marcus Crassus.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p:
Noble Ventidius, Whilst yet with Parthian blood thy sword is warm, The fugitive Parthians follow; spur through
Media, Mesopotamia, and the shelters whither The routed fly: so thy grand captain Antony Shall set thee on triumphant chariots and Put garlands on thy head.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p:
O Silius, Silius, I have done enough; a lower place, note well, May make too great an act: for learn this, Silius; Better to leave undone, than by our deed Acquire too high a fame when him we serve's
away. Cæsar and Antony have ever won More in their officer than person: Sossius, One of my place in Syria, his lieutenant, For quick accumulation of renown, Which he achieved by the minute, lost his favor. Who does i' the wars more than his captain can Becomes his captain's captain: and ambition, The soldier's virtue, rather makes choice of loss, Than gain which darkens him. I could do more to do Antonius good, But 'twould offend him; and in his offence Should my performance perish.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p:
Thou hast, Ventidius, that Without the which a soldier, and his sword, Grants scarce distinction. Thou wilt write to
Antony !

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I'll humbly signify what in his name, That magical word of war, we have effected; How, with his banners and his well-paid ranks, The ne'er-yet-beaten horse of Parthia We have jaded out o' the field.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Where is he now ?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p:
He purposeth to Athens: whither, with
what haste The weight we must convey with 's will permit, We shall appear before him. On there; pass
along! Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Rome. An ante-chamber in
Cæsar's house.

Enter AGRIPPA at one door, ENOBARBUS
at another.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: What, are the brothers parted ?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
They have dispatch'd with Pompey, he
is gone; The other three are sealing. Octavia weeps To part from Rome; Cæsar is sad; and Lepidus, Since Pompey's feast, as Menas says, is troubled With the green sickness.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: 'Tis a noble Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
A very fine one: O, how he loves
Cæsar !

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p:
Nay, but how dearly he adores Mark
Antony !

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Cæsar? Why, he's the Jupiter of men.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: What's Antony ? The god of Jupiter.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Spake you of Cæsar ? How! the
nonpareil !

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: O Antony ! O thou Arabian bird !

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Would you praise Cæsar, say 'Cæsar: '
go no further.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p:
Indeed, he plied them both with
excellent praises.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
But he loves Cæsar best; yet he loves
Antony: Ho! hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards,
poets, cannot Think, speak, cast, write, sing, number, ho! His love to Antony. But as for Cæsar, Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Both he loves.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
They are his shards, and he their beetle.
Trumpets within So; This is to horse. Adieu, noble Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p:
Good fortune, worthy soldier; and
farewell.
Enter CÆSAR, ANTONY, LEPIDUS, and OCTAVIA.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No further, sir.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
You take from me a great part of myself; Use me well in 't. Sister, prove such a wife As my thoughts make thee, and as my farthest
band Shall pass on thy approof. Most noble Antony, Let not the piece of virtue, which is set Betwixt us as the cement of our love, To keep it builded, be the ram to batter The fortress of it; for better might we Have loved without this mean, if on both parts This be not cherish'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Make me not offended In your distrust.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: I have said.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You shall not find, Though you be therein curious, the least cause For what you seem to fear: so, the gods keep you, And make the hearts of Romans serve your ends ! We will here part.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
Farewell, my dearest sister, fare thee
well: The elements be kind to thee, and make Thy spirits all of comfort! fare thee well.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.p: My noble brother !

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
The April 's in her eyes: it is love's
spring, And these the showers to bring it on. Be cheerful.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.p:
Sir, look well to my husband's house;
and-

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p:
What,
Octavia ?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.p: I'll tell you in your ear.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Her tongue will not obey her heart,
nor can Her heart inform her tongue,-the swan's
down-feather, That stands upon the swell at full of tide, And neither way inclines.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Will Cæsar weep ?

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: He has a cloud in 's face.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
He were the worse for
that, were he a horse; So is he, being a man.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Why, Enobarbus, When Antony found Julius Cæsar dead, He cried almost to roaring; and he wept When at Philippi he found Brutus slain.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
That year, indeed, he
was troubled with a rheum; What willingly he did confound he wail'd, Believe 't, till I wept too.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: No, sweet Octavia, You shall hear from me still; the time shall not Out-go my thinking on you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Come, sir, come; I'll wrestle with you in my strength of love : Look, here I have you; thus I let you go, And give you to the gods.

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Adieu; be happy!

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Let all the number of the stars give light To thy fair way!

sp.speaker: Cæs.
sp.p: Farewell, farewell! Kisses Octavia.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Farewell!

div.head: SCENE III
div.stage:
Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and
ALEXAS.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Where is the fellow ?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Half afeard to come.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Go to, go to.
Enter the Messenger as before.
Come hither, sir.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Good majesty, Herod of Jewry dare not look upon you But when you are well pleased.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
That Herod's head I'll have: but how, when Antony is gone Through whom I might command it ? Come
thou near.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Most gracious majesty,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Didst thou behold Octavia ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Ay, dread queen.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Where ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Madam, in Rome; I look'd her in the face, and saw her led Between her brother and Mark Antony.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Is she as tall as me ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: She is not, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Didst hear her speak ? is she
shrilltongued or low ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p:
Madam, I heard her speak; she is
low-voiced.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
That's not so good: he cannot like her
long.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Like her! O Isis! 'tis impossible.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
I think so, Charmian: dull of tongue,
and dwarfish! What majesty is in her gait? Remember, If e'er thou look'dst on majesty.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: She creeps: Her motion and her station are as one; She shows a body rather than a life, A statue than a breather.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Is this certain ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Or I have no observance.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Three in Egypt Cannot make better note.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: He's very knowing; I do perceive 't: there's nothing in her yet: The fellow has good judgment.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Guess at her years, I prithee.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Madam, She was a widow,—

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Widow! Charmian, hark.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: And I do think she's thirty.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
Bear'st thou her face in mind ? is't long
or round ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Round even to faultiness.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
For the most part, too, they are foolish
that are so. Her hair, what color ?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.p: Brown, madam: and her forehead As low as she would wish it.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: There's gold for thee. Thou must not take my former sharpness ill: I will employ thee back again; I find thee Most fit for business: go make thee ready; Our letters are prepared. Exit Messenger.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: A proper man.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Indeed, he is so: I repent me much That so I harried him. Why, methinks, by him, This creature's no such thing.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Nothing, madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p:
The man hath seen some majesty, and
should know.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Hath he seen majesty ? Isis else defend, And serving you so long!
